title: Tehran Refuses Nuclear Concessions as Gulf War Costs Soar Past $200 Billion
snippet: Iran's top security council declared Wednesday that Tehran will not surrender 'a single particle' of enriched uranium, dealing a fresh blow to U.S. peace terms as regional war costs and maritime chaos escalate.
content:
WASHINGTON — Tensions in the Middle East escalated on Wednesday as Iranian leaders firmly rejected U.S. demands to surrender the country's nuclear stockpile, even as the economic toll and infrastructure damage from the eight-month-old war continue to mount across the Persian Gulf.

Tehran Draws Hard Line on Uranium Stockpile

Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, declared via state media that Tehran will not permit the removal of "even a single particle of enriched nuclear material" from the country. The defiant stance directly conflicts with White House conditions for a ceasefire, which hinge on Iran relinquishing its enriched uranium and capping its nuclear capabilities.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly argued that military intervention was necessary to prevent Iran from building a bomb—an intention Tehran has consistently denied. Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reiterated Washington's resolve, stating that "crazy Islamists in Tehran will never ever have a nuclear weapon."

Staggering Economic Toll on Gulf Allies

While diplomatic talks stall, the financial fallout from the conflict is mounting rapidly for regional nations hosting U.S. forces. A report published Wednesday by insurer Allianz Trade estimated that physical damage across the Persian Gulf has already surpassed $200 billion, primarily concentrated in energy infrastructure across Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain.

More than 80 energy facilities have been hit since hostilities began, with nearly a third severely damaged. Allianz Trade warned that the cumulative economic loss for Gulf Cooperation Council nations could reach $790 billion by 2030, driven by output disruptions in energy, real estate, and tourism.

Strait of Hormuz Warfare and Global Sabotage

The conflict continues to threaten global shipping lanes. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed Wednesday that two more commercial oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines while trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz under U.S. military escort.

Beyond the Gulf, Western intelligence agencies allege Tehran is engaging in retaliatory covert operations. Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran's supreme leader, warned that nations assisting the U.S. naval blockade would face historical repercussions. French prosecutors recently attributed an October cyberattack targeting 700 French supermarkets—which spoiled tons of food and caused 20 fires—to Iranian operatives.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the accusations Wednesday while taunting Paris on social media, writing that a French government "unable to manage fridges" should not blame Tehran for its domestic failures.
